concept: Population, sample, discrete and continuous data
prompt:
A researcher records, for 80 students chosen at random from a school of 1200, their shoe size and the time they take to run 100 m.

**(a)** Identify the population and the sample. **[1]**

**(b)** Classify each variable as discrete or continuous. **[2]**
markscheme:
**(a)** Population: all 1200 students; sample: the 80 chosen **(A1)**

**(b)** Shoe size: discrete (only certain values, e.g. 6, 6.5, 7) **(A1)**; time: continuous (any value in a range, limited only by measurement) **(A1)**

prompt: To estimate how many hours per day teenagers spend online, a researcher posts a survey on a social media site. Explain why the results are likely to be biased.
markscheme: Only people who use that site (and choose to respond) can take part **(R1)**; they are likely to spend more time online than teenagers in general, so the estimate will probably be too high **(R1)**

prompt:
A data set has lower quartile 12 and upper quartile 20.

**(a)** Determine whether the value 35 is an outlier. **[2]**

**(b)** State what should be done before removing an outlier from a data set. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** IQR $=8$; upper boundary $20+1.5(8)=32$ **(M1)**; $35>32$, so it is an outlier **(A1)**

**(b)** Check whether it is an error (recording/measurement) or a genuine value; genuine extreme values should not simply be deleted **(R1)**

prompt:
A school has 480 students in Year 11 and 720 in Year 12. A sample of 50 students is to be taken.

**(a)** Find the number from each year in a stratified sample. **[2]**

**(b)** Explain one advantage of stratified sampling over simple random sampling here. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** Year 11: $\dfrac{480}{1200}\times50=20$; Year 12: $30$ **(M1)(A1)**

**(b)** Each year group is represented in proportion to its size, so the sample cannot by chance over-represent one year **(R1)**
